analysis.one_liner: Overhauls federal labor law to make unionizing easier, strike-breaking harder, and employer violations costlier.
analysis.headline: The bill has 217 cosponsors — all but two of them Democrats — but the House Education and Workforce Committee has taken no action since it was referred there on March 5, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act, the main federal law governing unions. It would make it harder for companies to label workers as independent contractors, treat franchisors and outsourcing firms as joint employers, override state right-to-work laws that let workers skip union fees, ban firing strikers or permanently replacing them, impose binding arbitration on companies that refuse to agree to a first union contract, void forced arbitration agreements that block class claims, and raise penalties on employers who violate labor law to as much as $50,000 per violation — double for repeat offenders — with personal liability for executives. The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and has sat there since.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want to join or form unions — including gig workers and franchise employees currently classified as contractors or treated as their franchisor's employees — gain faster elections, real penalties for employers who intimidate them, binding first contracts, and the right to strike without being permanently replaced. Existing union members in right-to-work states gain the ability to negotiate contracts requiring all covered workers to pay for representation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers seeking to unionize and union members

how_it_helps.text: Employers would be barred from permanently replacing strikers and from discriminating against workers who strike or return to work, and union-busting tactics like mandatory anti-union meetings would become unfair labor practices.

Union elections would have to be held within 20 business days of a petition, could be conducted by mail or electronically, and if the employer breaks the law and spoils an election, the Board could certify the union and order bargaining instead of holding a re-run.
Companies that stall first contracts would face mediation and then binding arbitration; the resulting contract would be imposed for two years.

Penalties for firing or coercing workers over union activity rise to as much as $50,000 per violation — doubled to $100,000 for repeat offenders — plus double liquidated damages, full back pay with no reductions, and a private right to sue with attorney's fees; executives who directed violations can be personally liable.
Forced arbitration agreements that block workers from joining class or collective claims over their employment would be unenforceable.

Fair-share fee agreements would be enforceable nationwide, overriding state right-to-work laws, and companies that share control over workers' terms (franchisors, outsourcers, platform companies) would be joint employers with bargaining duties.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who rely on outsourcing, franchising, contract labor, or anti-union management practices — retail and service chains, franchisors, staffing firms, and gig-economy platforms — would face higher labor costs, real penalties, and possible price or structure changes as a result.
analysis.who_pays_short: Outsourcers, franchisors, gig platforms, anti-union employers

drawbacks.text: The strict test for who counts as an employee could reclassify some independent contractors as employees, which would give them union and wage-law protections but could also cost some contractors scheduling flexibility, multiple-client arrangements, and independent business status — a real trade-off for gig workers on both sides.

Imposing a first contract by binding arbitration after roughly 120 days means the terms of a binding two-year contract can be set by a panel rather than negotiated, which business groups argue forces employers into terms they never agreed to.

Joint-employer liability and nationwide override of right-to-work laws would transfer costs and bargaining obligations onto franchisors and multi-state chains, which could be passed through to consumers or reflected in slower franchise hiring.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers strong, enforceable protections to workers who try to unionize, which is where most union campaigns die today — but it is an aggressive, one-size-fits-all rewrite. The contractor reclassification and forced first contracts are the provisions most likely to produce genuinely mixed results for some of the workers it aims to help. On the whole, the gains to workers organizing rights are large and the costs fall mainly on businesses with the most to lose from unionization.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has never held a markup or scheduled it for a vote, so it sits in committee while the Republican-led House moves on to other things.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia introduced the bill on March 5, 2025, with 217 original cosponsors.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Education and Workforce, and no further action — hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history.
Support is nearly universal among House Democrats: 215 of the 217 cosponsors are Democrats, with two Republicans, giving the bill a majority of the full House on paper.
The bill makes the NLRB's orders self-enforcing once issued, rather than requiring a court to approve enforcement, and adds new whistleblower protections for workers who report labor-law violations.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced the new unionization duties, penalties, and joint-employer liability are better off so far, since the bill has not moved; workers trying to organize are in the same legal position as they were in March 2025.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have faced new rules

sides.party_line_note: 215 of the bill's 217 cosponsors are Democrats and two are Republicans; the version of this bill in the previous Congress passed the House 225-206 on a near party-line vote, and this one has not gotten as far as a vote.

industries.note: The ABC test would force many platform and staffing workers into employee status, giving them collective bargaining and wage protections but ending the contractor arrangements their business models depend on. Some of those workers would gain rights; some would lose flexibility.

Joint-employer liability would make brands that dictate wages, scheduling, or policies through franchisees and contractors bargaining employers on the hook, removing a structure that keeps bargaining obligations away from the top of the chain.
The bill overrides state right-to-work laws, letting unions collect fees from all workers covered by their contracts, which strengthens union finances and bargaining leverage.
Every major mechanism — faster elections, bargaining orders, binding first contracts, penalties, fair-share fees — channels more workers and more money into union representation.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding the House majority and the Education and Workforce Committee having taken no action in the months since referral, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup or floor vote in this Congress; its realistic path is reintroduction with the next Congress, as its predecessors were.
